answer.text: conflict with the base pairing in the Watson and Crick model
answer.line: If adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equal. Extra adenine would leave some of it with no partner.

steps: Find the rule first. Paragraph 9, sentence 6: "if adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equally abundant."
Run the new case through it. Noticeably more adenine than thymine means some adenine has no thymine to face.
That breaks the pairing in the Watson and Crick model. Rule first, then the case.

choices.text: have a correspondingly lower proportion of guanine than of cytosine
choices.note: Nothing ties an adenine surplus to guanine and cytosine. That pairing is separate, and the choice invents a trade-off between the two.

choices.text: confirm the tetranucleotide hypothesis proposed by Levene
choices.note: Levene's fixed repeat of four bases means equal amounts of each. Extra adenine cuts against that too, and paragraph 3 already retired the idea.

choices.text: conflict with the base pairing in the Watson and Crick model
choices.note: One adenine faces one thymine, so a surplus of adenine has nowhere to go.

choices.text: have a double helix whose diameter is wider than 20 angstroms
choices.note: Diameter came from Photo 51 and is never tied to base counts. The equal pair widths in paragraph 9 point the other way.

choices.text: support Pauling's three-chain structure for the molecule
choices.note: Pauling's model appears only as a flawed three-chain attempt. Nothing links it to base ratios.
